claims.text: Inducing in situ formation of nanoscale ceramic precipitates within a high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
The initial as-cast high-entropy alloy has a primarily homogeneous microstructure.
Tailored heat treatment or thermomechanical processing can precipitate nanoscale ceramic phases such as TiC uniformly within the alloy.
The proposed improvement should operate at approximately 800–1000°C under static and cyclic loading.
The processing intervention will form uniformly dispersed nanoscale ceramic precipitates along grain boundaries.
The processing intervention will form nanoscale ceramic precipitates within grains.
Ceramic precipitates along grain boundaries will pin the boundaries.
Intragranular ceramic precipitates will hinder dislocation motion.
The ceramic precipitates will impede grain-boundary sliding at high temperatures.
Impeded grain-boundary sliding and dislocation motion will delay high-temperature creep deformation.
Impeded grain-boundary sliding and dislocation motion will increase high-temperature yield strength relative to the unmodified alloy.
Compared with the as-cast state, the treated alloy will exhibit improved high-temperature yield strength.
Compared with the as-cast state, the treated alloy will exhibit reduced high-temperature creep rates.
The improvement is expected to persist in extreme thermal environments up to approximately 1000°C.
Long-term stability under extended thermal cycling has not been validated.
A greater than 10% increase in yield strength is offered as an example of a statistically significant improvement.
